q: A bot in a team chat starts treating messages like "lgtm" and "taking lunch" as task requests. What is the likely cause?
options: dmPolicy set to "allowlist"
groupPolicy set to "open"
Triage routed to a small model
GitHub push events in the watch list
explanation: An open group policy makes every channel message an event. Without group chat rules in SOUL.md, casual talk reads as work.

q: An agent has a rule that treats organize, sort, and clean-up requests as requests for a plan. The user asks it to "organize my project folder." What should the agent do first?
options: Move files by type, then report what changed
Refuse, because organizing is destructive
State its interpretation, give counts and examples, and ask to proceed
Delete duplicate files only, since that is low risk
explanation: The added rule treats organize, sort, and clean up as requests for a plan. The agent previews counts and 5 to 10 examples before changing anything.

q: An agent separates draft review from send approval. The operator replies "looks good" to a drafted client email. What happens?
options: The agent sends the email
The agent treats it as review approval and waits for an explicit "send"
The agent queues the email for the next heartbeat to send
The agent discards the draft
explanation: Approval words confirm the draft stage only. Sending requires a confirmation that uses the word send.

q: During an unattended heartbeat, an agent sends a client an unapproved invoice reminder. MEMORY.md contains "send Acme a reminder Friday." Which was NOT a contributing cause?
options: Send permission with no confirmation gate
A memory entry phrased as a direct instruction
Heartbeats having the same tool access as operator turns
A prompt injection hidden in a client email
explanation: The agent followed its own stored instruction. No injection was involved.

q: An agent told once to "connect with relevant agents" keeps contacting other agents for days. Why?
options: The goal sat in MEMORY.md as ongoing, so every turn and heartbeat re-evaluated it
A flaw in its HTTP skill was exploited
The operator approved each contact
Other agents edited its SOUL.md
explanation: Open-ended goals stored as in-progress keep firing. Without a trust hierarchy or scope limit, the agent keeps acting.

q: Which fix most reliably prevents the inbox deletion pattern?
options: A confirmation gate for all deletes in AGENTS.md
A scope-clarification rule in SOUL.md
Removing delete permissions entirely
Re-authorizing with narrower OAuth scopes
explanation: Without delete permission the agent cannot delete under any instruction. In production, still apply all four fixes as defense in depth.

q: Why is the inbox deletion pattern not an edge case?
options: Gmail's API always skips the Trash folder
Most users phrase requests maliciously
Models are trained to favor deletion
All four required conditions exist in a default deployment
explanation: Default delete permission, no gate, a silent SOUL.md, and a natural vague request together make the outcome predictable.

q: After an incident, a team rebuilds its agent config. Where should every confirmation requirement live?
options: AGENTS.md
SOUL.md
openclaw.json channel settings
MEMORY.md
explanation: AGENTS.md holds the per-tool operational rules the runtime enforces. SOUL.md stays a lean identity file.

q: In a two-agent pipeline, drafts sometimes cite incomplete research because the router sends work to the research and writing agents at once. What's the fix?
options: Sanitize footnotes in drafts
Make research completion a precondition for drafting
Block the research agent from sending email
Merge back to one agent to save cost
explanation: The tasks are sequential, not independent. Routing must respect the dependency.

q: In a research-and-writing pipeline, what is the main reason to split research and writing into separate agents?
options: To use different messaging channels
To let the Writing Agent browse the web
Context isolation, so drafts start clean with only the needed research
To meet a regulatory requirement
explanation: Separate contexts kept accumulated research history from diluting drafts and also lowered cost.
